nodes.label: Analysis
nodes.question: What shift in cocoa farming practices has been observed since the promotion of hybrid cocoa varieties?
nodes.answer: There has been a shift away from traditional shaded cocoa agroforestry systems towards full-sun monocrop cocoa plantations.
nodes.paragraph: Agriculture has contributed to around a third of all deforestation in the region around Ekiti (Olorun- femi et al. 2020). Since the 1980s, the creation and distribution of hybrid cocoa varieties across much of West Africa promoted the use of full-sun monocrop cocoa plantations (World Agroforestry 2021), push- ing a strong narrative of modernization with the ulti- mate aim of increasing yields (Kolavalli and Vigneri 2011). This shift away from traditional shaded cocoa agroforestry systems, which integrate trees with cocoa crops has been observed to a large extent on the ground (Ruf 2011; Hutchins et al. 2015). However, in Nigeria, some researchers such as Lokpobiri (2019) noted a failed translation of federal policy to state- level implementation due to issues such as a lack of commitment, consistency, and falsification (Ojong and Anam 2018; Lokpobiri 2019). nodes.question: What is agroforestry and why has it become a topic of interest?
nodes.answer: Agroforestry is the practice of integrating trees with agricultural crops, and it has gained interest as a climate change mitigation measure due to its ability to retain trees and regulate micro-climates, as well as provide diversified income streams.

Full-sun cocoa plantations can degrade soil fertility and biodiver - sity which impacts crop health and decreases resil- ience (Ariza-Salamanca et al. 2023; Tondoh et al. 2015; Bennett et al. 2021). Full-sun systems have also been found to stop producing cocoa at a younger age (Andres et al. 2016; Wessel and Quist-Wessel 2015). Agroforestry has therefore become a topic of interest as both a climate change mitigation measure through its retention of trees as well as an adaptation measure through regulation of micro-climates (e.g., shading cocoa from direct sunlight) and provision of diversi- fied income streams (Jagoret et al. 2019). With proper management, agroforestry systems can have 10 times the total system output (when non-cocoa harvests are included) compared to their full-sun counterparts, potentially contributing to greater food and income security (Niether et al. 2020; Jezeer et al. 2017). nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What regions in West Africa were involved in the studies distinguishing agroforestry cocoa systems from full-sun counterparts?
nodes.answer: The studies were conducted in Ghana and Cameroon.
nodes.paragraph: 2020; Benefoh et al. 2018). When this study was conducted, only three studies in West Africa (Ghana and Cameroon) had been able to distinguish agrofor - estry cocoa systems from their full-sun counterparts (Ashiagbor et al. 2020; Numbisi et al. 2019; Benefoh et al. 2018). While of great scientific relevance, the methods used in those studies have limited spatial accuracy or public accessibility due to the use of com- mercial satellite imagery. This has resulted in limited applicability for cocoa land use planning (Ashiagbor et al. 2020), and understanding of the current level of climate change adaptation in Nigeria. Since this study was conducted, there have been some further developments in this area (such as Moraiti et al. 2024; Kanmegne Tamga et al. 2023). That said, mapping in Nigeria has continued to be limited. A recent map- ping exercise conducted by CHUSSDEV (2023) in Cross River State, has emphasized the importance of accurate mapping to address challenges such as forest and biodiversity loss faced by the sector.
